en: Having diligently undertaken the supreme arrangement of shrines, temples, monasteries, and so forth, one should determine their length,
breadth, and circumference, even for those that are circular.
Regarding the supreme exertion in the proper maintenance of what has been newly constructed, such as stūpas, guest houses, and monasteries: [this concerns] the *gaṇḍī*,
the staff, the top [of the pole], the standing [position], the door, the pillars, and the wood for the *jātaka* [sculptures].
Having deliberated upon all that, the measurement was determined by the master builders, architects, and others.

Without taking up a formal position, [the master]—having fully deliberated upon their dimensions with all the details such as the *gaṇḍī*, the life-tree (*srog shing*), and the pinnacle; the doors and so forth; the pillars, the supporting beams (*bskyed pa'i shing*), the width, the depth, and the circularity; the lords of the site, and the drawing of the lines—should set out on the journey to the grove (*vanayātrā*) together with the carpenters. This is in *āryā* meter.
Having gathered all necessary materials and observed an auspicious day marked by favorable stars and planets, he [proceeded].

"O disciples, let us go together with the preceptors to behold the wonders of the forest. Having examined the auspicious conjunctions of the constellations, planets, and days, the mantra-practitioner who has brought an end to obstacles should enter a remote region of the delightful mountain forests in the north-easterly direction, having observed the proper time."
The mantrin, having assumed the form of Yamāntaka and carefully observed the time, should face the northeast and enter a forest, a mountain, or a most excellent and delightful site.
Those trees that have dense branches growing in a favorable location, possess a very glossy appearance with dark, red, or yellow hues,
and are rich with fragrant flowers and milky sap accompanied by very sweet fruits, are suitable.
Born in an excellent location, lovely and lush, possessing colors of green, blue, red, and yellow, endowed with sweet fruit and fragrant flowers,
rich in milk, with fully developed branches and leaves— such upright trees are indeed possessed of quality, species, and age.
By birth, they are young men ranging from one hundred years up to two hundred years of age.

Branches and leaves were fully developed, and they were endowed with excellent qualities, noble species, and fine timber. Having grown for more than a hundred years and up to two hundred years, they were in the prime of their life.
These included *puṃnāga*, *nāgakesara*, *śrīpāsa*, *aśvattha*, *śiṃśapā*, and *aśoka*;
as well as *jambū*, *palāśa*, *candana*, *kiṃśuka*, *kaṅkelli*, *tāla*, *śāla*, and *āmra* trees.

The *sumanāga* tree, the *nāgakeśara*, the *śrīśīsa*, the *aśvattha*, the *śiṃśapā*, the *nirvāṇa*, the *jambū*, the *pīluśa*, *candana*, *kiṃśuka*, *kaṅkelli*, *tāla*, *sāla*, *āmra*, *campaka*, *bilva*, *kucandana*, *vaihaṅkata*, *bakula*, *rohiṇī*, *khadira*, *śrīparṇa*, *tindusāra*, *kramuka*, *arjuna*, *devadāru*, *vaṭa*, and *jāta*.

*Tsambaka*, *bilva*, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), *bījakataka*, *bakula*, *rohiṇī*, *khadira*, *śrīparṇa*, *hintāla*, *śaraka*, *madhūka*, *arjuna*, *devadāru*, and the *pāṭali* species—these are suitable for construction works; however, those who are children, the elderly, or those with crooked limbs are not.
A child is one up to one hundred years of age, and those over two hundred years are the elderly.

These are those suitable for tasks such as building palaces and the like; they are not those who are too young, too old, or have deformed limbs. "Too young" refers to one who has not reached one hundred years of age; "too old" refers to one who has exceeded two hundred years.
With their branches withered, severed, or singed, their leaves scorched and their limbs shattered;
growing in cremation grounds, pits, caves, temples, and along roads, they are pungent and bitter.
Dry, solitary, with broken branches, scorched, with withered leaves, and shattered limbs; grown in charnel grounds, pits, ravines, divine abodes, or on roads;
scorched, cold, or situated in impure regions; born at the edges of ponds or rivers; those consumed alone;
those dwelling in the nests of birds or serpents; those struck by lightning, perforated by insects, or left as remnants.

Having avoided those dwelling in places where villagers were not permitted to enter, those born on the banks of lakes or rivers, those of the size of birds or reptiles, and those that had been shattered by the blow of a thunderbolt— having thus excluded them, and having searched among them with skillful effort but not seeing him, he then, at the time of twilight, protected the mountain Bhadra from all sides along with his companions, the artisan carpenters.

Among those [trees], the most excellent and auspicious species are to be examined here. Furthermore, at the time of the junctions (*saṃdhyā*), the carpenters together with the craftsmen must be properly guarded;
one should be full of enthusiasm, possessing the yoga of Amṛtakuṇḍalin according to the ritual of the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāravidhi*).
Having fully worshipped the Sugata together with his sons, as well as all the guardians of the directions, the forest deities, and the tree spirits;

Possessing the yoga of the Amṛtakuṇḍalī and with great enthusiasm, one should perfectly worship the Sugatas together with their sons, as well as the deities of the directions and the deities of the forest trees, by means of the five types of sensory enjoyments.
Having satisfied his assistants and artisans with offerings of food, drink, and oblations to the quarters,
the mantra-practitioner should address the Sugatas and deities with the verses beginning with "O Blessed One."

Having offered the directional *bali* cakes, one should fully satisfy the mantra-practitioners together with the artisans with food and drink, and then offer prayers to the Sugatas and the deities with verses beginning with "Bhagavan," and so forth.
With a joyful mind and a tranquil heart, one should sleep through the power of perfected yoga;
in a good dream there is complete accomplishment, while in a bad dream, the mantra for all rites should be recited.

One should sleep with a mind of intense joy, a tranquil intellect, and through non-dual yoga. If the dream is auspicious, there will be perfect accomplishment; if the dream is inauspicious, one should perform the recitation of the *sarvakarmika* [mantra].
The illustrious yogin Vairocana, at dawn, having performed all the offerings,
worshipped the King of Trees (the Bodhi tree) in its form as the deities residing within it, such as the guardians of the quarters.

Early in the morning, through the yoga of Vairocana together with the intermediate state, one should properly worship the deities in the form of the directional guardians who reside upon that king of trees, fully endowed with all offerings:
Śāle, Śarale, Tilase, and Dāru, as well as the goddess Lokamātrikā and the field-protector named Mahāmeru who resides there.
The goddess who perfectly dwells upon the śāla, mango, and sesame trees is the Mother of the World; and the field-protector who dwells there is this one called Mahāmeru.
The goddess Guhyakā resides among the *puṃnāga*, *nāgakesara*, *campā*, and *aśoka* trees;
there also dwells the protector of the field named Mahābala, who provides protection.
Sumāṅga, Nāgakeśara, Campaka, and Aśoka are the secret mothers of the goddesses, and their powerful field-protectors are known as the Great Strengths (Mahābala).

Hārītakī is the cause of Hārītī at the banyan tree; Karṇamoṭikā is the cause at the mango tree; Ambikā and Anala are the causes at the palmyra tree; and Śaṅkarikā and Ūrdhvakeśa are also [the causes] there.
On the *āruṣka* tree, there is *karṇamoṭikā* and *hetu*; on the *tūta* tree, there is *āmbikā* and *phala*; on the *tāla* tree, there is *śaṅkhari* and *ūrdhvakeśī*.
At the *kadamba* tree dwells the goddess Sumukhā; at the *karañja*, the goddess Karañjavāsinī;
the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*) is Mahāghaṇṭa; and at the *madhuka*, Puṃseśvara Śekā.
On the *kadamba* tree resides the goddess Bzang-mo; on the *mṛdvīkā* tree resides the goddess Mṛdvīkā-sthā; the lords of the fields are Mahāghaṇṭā; on the *madhu* tree reside Puruṣeśvara and Śāśā.
On the *kāñcana* tree is the goddess Caṇḍālī and the field-protector Sujanetrā;
on the *śālmali* is the great goddess Agnivaktrā and on the *śākhoṭa* is Kāminī and Bhīma;
on the peaks is Mahālakṣmī and the lord of the field named Vahnimukha.

On the golden tree are the goddess Caṇḍā and the field-protector Sujāta. On the śālmali tree is the great goddess Agnimukhī, and on the staraka tree is Kāmā; these field-protectors are fearsome. On the śrīgaja tree are Mahāsampadā and the field-protector known as Agnimukha.
The names of these [deities], along with their locations and other such distinctions, have not been stated here due to the fear of excessive prolixity.
Their arms, colors, weapons, and mantras should be ascertained with effort from other tantras.
Today I am prepared to cut down a tree for the purpose of building a monastery and other such structures.
"I must now be forgiven by you; you should dwell instead at another tree.
Today I am willing to cut down trees for the sake of the monastery and other such needs; therefore, please grant me your forgiveness now and reside at another tree."
Otherwise, having worshipped all the deities who have arrived at an old tree with special offerings, worship, and so forth, one should spend the moment conceived as the form of Vighnāntaka.
One should properly worship all the deities who have gone to other elder trees with specific offerings such as bali-offerings and the like.
Having gratified [the deity] with drinks, food, betel, garlands, sandalwood, garments, and gold,
one should smear the axe for cutting with honey using the upper right hand.

One should properly propitiate a woodcutter who has the form of Vighnāntaka with drinks, food, tooth-cleansers, garlands, sandalwood, garments, and gold; then, having thoroughly smeared the edge of the axe with vajra-honey, one should praise him with the right hand.
Facing east or north and looking at the sun, one should recite the *Śrīmāyūrī* protection with a virtuous mind, making it the primary assistance.
With a virtuous mind, facing northeast and looking toward the sun, one should perform the cutting. For the sake of protecting the primary co-emergent ones, the glorious Mahāmāyūrī should be recited.
The great counselor should examine from all sides the signs of what is beneficial and what is harmful;
the wise man should abandon that which is harmful and practice everything that is beneficial.
% What is this?

% The great mantra practitioner should thoroughly examine all signs, whether they are superior or inferior. If they are inferior, they should be abandoned; if they are superior, the wise one should worship them all perfectly.
If the fall occurs in the northern direction, it indicates the success of the donor's wealth and actions;
a fall in the northeast corner (aiśānakoṇa) should be known to indicate the attainment of knowledge.

If [the body] falls toward the northern direction, it indicates that the donor will achieve wealth, the fulfillment of their activities, and so forth. If it falls toward the direction of Ishana (the northeast), it indicates the attainment of vidyā, primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and the like.
If a tree falls in the direction of Indra (the east), it indicates specific victory, prosperity,
and excellence; however, if it falls in another intermediate direction without being obstructed, it portends happiness and well-being.
If it is situated in the fire [direction], there is fear of Vaiśvānara; if it has gone to the direction of the Lord of the Dead (Yama), it indicates death.
There is fear of disease in the southwest (Nairṛta); if it goes to the water or wind [directions], there is fear of water and wind.

In the direction of Fire, there is the fear of fire. If one goes toward the direction of the Lord of Pretas (Yama), it indicates death. In the direction of the Devoid of Truth (Nairṛta), there is the fear of disease. If one goes toward Water and Wind, there is the fear of water and wind.
If it crushes another tree, it portends danger to its master;
if it flies far away, cries out, or trembles, it brings suffering to the giver.
If one goes while being distressed by another tree, it indicates the fear of a master. If one trembles and weeps while falling a long distance, the giver will experience suffering.
From seeing dogs, camels, snakes, pigs, jackals, donkeys, crows, vultures, or wicked people at the time of the eclipse, there will be fear, imprisonment, and obstacles.
At the time of performing *gcod*, if one sees dogs, camels, snakes, pigs, wolves, donkeys, crows, or vultures—those who are malevolent—the fear of being bound and many obstacles will arise.
If blood flows from a tree when it is cut, it portends the death of the donor;
if curd, ghee, honey, or milk flow, it portends fear of execution or imprisonment.
If blood flows from the tree when it is cut, it indicates death and other such calamities for the donor. If curd, ghee, honey, or milk emerge, it indicates the terrors of being killed or bound.
When there is a sweet-astringent taste and a clear, dark, fragrant smell, a natural stream of saliva flows without effort; this is considered auspicious.

The natural state of sustenance consists of the flavors of sweet and bitter and so forth, as well as purity, ritual purification, the inhalation of fragrant scents, and the continuous flow of unctuous tastes.
Just as one observes the distinctions of color and form when a tree is cut down,
those who know causes declare that the internal form [of the embryo] corresponds to those very distinctions of color and form.

Whatever distinction of color is seen in the wood held by the cutter, from that distinction of the appearance of its color, the nature of the core is indicated through the knowledge of its causal signs:
from [the colors] madder-red, tawny, yellow, dove-grey, owl-grey, rhinoceros-brown, blood-red, and dark-green;
by the marks of the madder-red color, a frog or a disease is inferred.

From those that are the color of saffron, pale yellow, yellow, the color of a pigeon, the color of a sword, red, and dark blue; from the mark of the saffron color, one should recognize it as a tortoise, but that does not exist.

From stealing a brown mouse from its nest, one incurs the state of being a thief, a dog, or afflicted by disease; from stealing a yellow one, one is born as a monitor lizard, and thereafter one falls into poverty.
From yellowish-white [dust], mice arise within; they cause the occurrence of thieves and diseases of the lungs. From yellow [dust], precious objects arise; these also cause the loss of wealth.
From a dove comes a house-lizard; from that, indeed, comes poverty for the master.
From a partridge comes a chameleon, and because of that, various diseases arise here.

From the color of a pigeon, there is wealth in the household, yet by that [color], the king is made poor. From the color of a greyish-white [dove], there is longevity; by that, one will suffer various diseases here.
From a dark-colored [snake], the birth of a serpent occurs; by that, there is a great loss of wealth for the donor.
Due to a difference in color like that of a sword, there is water and danger from it.
From a dark blue [complexion], a nāga emerges, and by that, the wealth of the great donor is exhausted. From a distinction in the color of a sword, water arises, and from it, fear will occur.
It is highly auspicious, marked with the signs of the Śrīvatsa, the Vardhamānaka, the Nandyāvarta, the wheel, the svastika, the lotus, the parasol, the goad, the jar, the banner, and the chowrie.
The glorious *vatsa*,
*vardhamāna*, *nandyāvarta*, *cakra*, *svastika*, *padma*, *chattra*, *aṅkuśa*, *kalaśa*, *dhvaja*, and *vyajana* are taught as the marks of greatness (*mahālakṣaṇa*).
Having thus thoroughly examined all this, both auspicious and inauspicious, the wise Great Master should then cause the excellent tree to be cut and split.

Having thoroughly examined all such virtuous and non-virtuous [actions], the great master should cut and fashion [the wood] to that same extent; the wise one should perform this upon the best of trees.

Having removed the knots from the root, tip, and middle sections, and having observed them on all sides, the entire length should be made ten percent greater than the measurement in every respect. ||o||

Having gazed at all the *śalākā* (counting sticks) in the central portion, from the base to the tip, one should perform [the calculation] for all of them, increasing by one-tenth in every measurement and so forth.
Then, having thoroughly understood the specific configuration of the stones required to construct a shrine (caitya) and other edifices,
[one should seek] a site hidden by mountains, ridges, riverbanks, excellent bathing-ghats, divine enjoyments, and trees.

Then, for the purpose of accomplishing [the construction of] stūpas and so forth, one must thoroughly understand the specific characteristics of excellent stones: those found in mountain valleys, on the banks of rivers, at auspicious confluences, or among trees frequented by deities;
as well as those from caves, Devendra, Dhanada, Paśupati, Brahmā, Sāsaṅga, and Mūrdhanī.
Stones that face the east, north, or south are praised.
Stones that have fallen from above while in association with the Lord of Gods, Vaiśravaṇa, Paśupati, and Brahmā, and which face toward the east, the north, or upward, are praised.
The eastern direction bestows one's own desires; the northern direction generates sons, daughters, and lineage;
the northeastern direction grants the fruit of liberation; and the upward direction is the accomplishment of the *khecarī* siddhi for all aims.

A site near a shrine, an assembly hall, a cremation ground, or a crossroads; scorched by the rays of the morning sun; attached to an anthill or a tree; multicolored; and unworked—such a site should be abandoned.

One should discard stones that are near a stūpa, in a charnel ground, at a crossroads, red in color, or those that have been quickly moved, or those attached to anthills, or those of many colors, or those used for other purposes.
A gem that has the mixed luster of bell-metal and vimala brings death to the giver; likewise, one with gold brings death.
One that is white, yellow, or red in color, yet marked by a black line, causes harm.

One that is like stainless rock-salt causes death to the donor; it will bring about his slaughter. Among those that are white, yellow, and red in color, one that possesses black markings is defective;
therefore, one should avoid her whose signs of pregnancy are seen, as she is full of many faults.
There are four types of *śilāja* (bitumen): the young, the adolescent, the middle-aged, and the old.
Whoever perceives signs as being the essence should abandon them, for they possess many faults. The four types—infants, youths, middle-aged, and the elderly—are the vajra families.
A young woman who is extremely soft, when struck by the hammer, endures only the brick itself;
an old woman who is rough, discolored, and devoid of voice is like a poor-quality stone and is to be censured.
The child is exceedingly soft; through patient training, he becomes like a son to his father. The elder is harsh, ill-favored in appearance, and devoid of melodic voice; like a tortoise, he is base.

The middle-aged woman possesses the quality of firmness; she is fragrant, has a deep voice, and is cool. She is dense, firm yet tender, youthful, very smooth, and bestows desire; she is the most excellent.

The middle [part] possesses subtle qualities; it is fragrant, has a deep sound, is cool, and is firm. Firmness, softness, and extreme smoothness constitute youth, which is supreme because it bestows desire.
White, yellow, green, red, and dark-blue in luster, endowed with beauty and youth;
or else, the letters of the mantras and so forth should be known as distinguished by the various classes such as the *jāti* and others.

Possessing the colors and radiance of white, yellow, green, red, and dark blue, and endowed with youthfulness, one should recognize the distinctions of lineage and so forth, and then offer praise through mantras and other means.
If the auspicious black stone is marked with white lines and joined with fine dots, it brings joy through a daughter; such is the rule.
Even if a stone is of good quality but black, if it is perfectly endowed with fine white lines and spots, it will become possessed of intelligence and kin.
Thus concludes the ritual of the forest grove.
